Did you get that car finished?
It was finished all the time. The battery is...

Got it going again for another... That last reel the train went by. For a while there was a cricket. Was that a... That's to play? No, no, no, he'll play it in another... We'll run through him. We'll use other boxes. If you want to talk a few more minutes, there's about a half an hour on each table. If you don't want to go the whole half hour, we can stop. Oh, I mean, I'll talk.

I mean, you can... I'll tell you about this Shake Up Melindsay fellow. That's what I was going to tell you one time about Shake Up Melindsay. I'll come to meet him. He had gotten sick, see? So all the musicians, they got together and they decided that they would give a party and it all pay for nothing. And they would give, you know, all the proceeds to him. So that's how I come to meet Shake Up Melindsay. What part of town did he come from? He, I think he came from across the river someplace. I didn't know too much of him. But his mother had just lately moved next door to us. I think she had bought the house, see? But before that, they had came from across the river, I think. And so they gave the party. And at that party, they had a whole gang of trumpet players there. And you would have enjoyed hearing that. And these was the trumpeters that they had there. They had Sam Morgan. They had Kid Rainy. They had Shake Up Melindsay. They had Punch. They had Philip Moreri. Philip Moreri, he played there. Now that was a guy. He's the guy that played Panama. He's the guy composed at Panama. And he got killed. He was trying to hold boys the way to Chicago. That's the way. Because he was going up that way to, that's the way that most of the guys, you know, they didn't make much money. And if they had any way of getting someplace with their instruments or their horn, they'd get there. If it was danger, they didn't mind danger. They was going to get there. See? And he got killed. And his trumpet was crushed inside of him. But he was the guy who played this number, Panama. And if they check up on it, you ain't going to never find the fellow who composed Panama. Because he was the guy, because I had put some part of the lyrics, I mean the music to it, because he liked it, that part that was one of the numbers that I made when I was a little kid. I was about, oh, I was about, about nine then. And I had composed a little blues. And I called it Albert Blues, because my name is Albert Broussard, see? And he used a part of those blues to put in Panama. And I remember well that they said he had composed that music because there was a piano player. Oh, he was much of a piano player. They called him Cross-Eyed George for a nickname. I don't know what his real name is. I think his name was George Harris. I think it was Harris. But they called him Cross-Eyed George. And oh, he could play a piano. And Phillip Moreri was playing along with him when I first heard him. Well, Phillip Moreri was one of the guys that was at the party. And it was all contests. And that's where the joy came in. When he would hit that high note, when he was playing Panama, he'd go way down there. And he'd say he had that number. Ta-da! Ta-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da! And he'd just keep that note over and over. And it was really thrilling to hear him play that number. And then this fellow Punch would blow the same number because they had all gotten into it because it was really a good number. And they all had a little piece of that number, but he had a master. See? He didn't have the reputation that they had because he was a newcomer then. But he was making it warm for them. And he was sitting down there enjoying it and everybody was over there and he was just a youngster. He was blowing up some trumpet. I mean, our judge at that time, Phillip must have been about 19 years old, 19 or 20 years old. They called him Phillip Moreri. And he played much piano. And that's why I heard Shake Up My Lens. And when he got to make it warm, then he came there with that number. Ta-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. And that was his main number with Shake Up My Lens. And that's where I had first saw some of the good musicians. And Ory was there. And he was a trombone player at that time. And who else was there? And I can't think of this other trumpet. Oh, yeah. Cabone. Frank Cabone was there. He was the guy. He played music on progressive jazz now. He was always a half note in front of the music that you was playing. But the way that he played it, oh, man, he was really strong with it. He only died recently. He was one of my uncles. What was the name again? Frank Thompson. Frank Thompson. Frank Thompson. Now, he played quite a few jobs around his town. He really, he had cornbread quite a lot. And he had Big Al. Do you know Big Al? Oh, yeah. Big Al. Guitar player? Yeah, guitar player. Well, Big Al and him, Big Al used to play guitar for him.
Did you mention Carbone did you say?
Yeah, Carbone. We used to call him Kev. Frank Carbone. It was a nickname that we gave him. His name was Frank Thomas, see? But we called him Frank Carbone. Oh, yeah.
You talk about Big Bill's brother? Big Bill's brother.
Oh, yeah.
I played with Frank. Sure.
Yeah, Frank Carbone. And he really played nice trumpet.

He worked for Lettler, Ye, and Phillip. He worked for Lettler, Ye, and Phillip. That's right. And he... He used to live on St. Peter, between me and I talked to you. Right next door to us. Across the street from Stanko. Across the street from Stanko. From Stanko.
That's where we were living. That's right. Right across from Stanko. That's where...
There's a lot of jobs with him. Oh, man.
He really could play.
He was one of them that... I'll tell you who he admired. He admired Chris Kelly, because he could play the blues. Oh!
That's the guy I was trying to think about.
He could play the blues. Frank could play the blues.

That's the trumpet player. He's the guy that was known for playing Kellis Love. That's the way I would tell him. He was one of the main elements at Jacob Melendez's party. Now, Chris Kelly was the guy. He could sit right here with that little short brass trumpet he had. Cornet. Cornet, yeah. That's what it... It wasn't... Looked like it was just about 12 inches long. And that guy would sit down as I blow this imitation. That's the way I got an idea of blowing this imitation of the trumpet. I tried to sound my notes, because he used to sound his notes so low. He could take that trumpet and sit in the corner of the room where he was, and he'd sound like he was a mile away. Yeah. And he could blow... He was strictly a blues player on a trumpet. He played CC Rider, Don't You Feel My Legs. And he played... What's this other... Blue Monday Blues. And he was strictly a blues... Kellis Love, that was his favorite number. He used to play that Kellis Love. And I played the piano behind him. And... Where, Howard, is he gone? Yeah. I wanted to make him get me a little wash down so I could have bowed that... This is the way he used to blow that trumpet. This is what he used to play. And I imitated. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ ¶¶ How could you love someone else, baby, and don't care for me? . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . this imitation a little bit. At one time I could blow an imitation of a trumpet just as clear as any trumpet. That sounds good now. And it's in bad shape and right now I should have drank a drink of water or something like that, which I haven't drank water all day. I've been fooling around with these chords and with a wet mouth vocal and I can blow out a trumpet tune as clear as a trumpet. I'd blow all that, see like Levene Rose and all those numbers like that, Harry Jane's numbers, I'd blow that imitation of trumpet. That's what would make me uh raid so much along in the party, see. If I didn't have the trumpet player, well I'd just get on there and blow the trumpet with my mouth, see. And uh that's uh that'd be a terrific hit, see. I want to ask you, do you
remember uh uh Willie Webber used to live on Mero Street, the trumpet player? He used to be a Slater?

Yeah, yeah, Willie Webber. He was, he was long in the middle. That was, that was my, my aunt's brother-in-law. He was a good trumpet player. Yeah, my, my uncle married his sister, Willie Webber, yeah. They got so many of the trumpet players, they had real good trumpeters way back there. Many of them, they haven't came to my mind yet, you know. Speaking of trumpet players, do you remember Buddy Petit? Yeah, yes. Buddy Petit was real good. He was one of the top notches, Buddy Petit. Buddy Petit, Louis Armstrong, Kid Rainey, and Kid Punch, Sam Morgan. Those was the guys who used to back them wagons up there and they'd contest against each other. One, it was just a matter of opinion. See, now you see like Louis Armstrong would be blowing uh those high notes. Rainey used to blow in the KSC. Yeah. But uh, towards the late years, I mean he played people with him towards the late years, but he wasn't near as good when he was young because he had took to drinking, you know. He had gave it up for a time, see. And uh... He wasn't as good in his late years, you said. No, he wasn't half as good. That guy blew a trumpet. Oh, he blew a trumpet. I mean it was... You know uh, who uh, took pattern after him? You ever hear Sharky Banana? Yeah. Sharky Banana used to come and sit and listen to him. Now Sharky Banana, Rainey used to give Sharky Banana ideas. Louis Armstrong would give Louis Prima ideas. Now uh, uh, Sharky Banana, their name was Montgomery. He had a brother that was a real good drummer. They called Roy Montgomery. Oh, yeah. Yeah, he was a real good drummer, see. Well, he gave up the drums. I mean he was supposed to give it up. And um, he used to follow behind Benny. They had a guy they called Benny. He was the guy who first started putting all those different kind of gadgets. You see, like he used to play the tiger rag and hold that tiger at uh, at the lyric show. And when you say hold the tiger, he had a big old hat box with a cord and you pull it and make the tiger holler. He was a drummer. And he... Black Benny. Black Benny. That's they called him. Black Benny.
What did he do to make the tiger holler?

He had a big round hat box with a cord rising and he pull it and say, hold that tiger. Ooh, hold that tiger. Ooh, hold that tiger. And he'd be pulling and playing all the time. Yeah, and he'd pull it and he'd play. And the tiger rag was a famous rag at that time, the tiger rag. And I used to play all them kind of, all them kind of numbers. Of course, I mean, you know, uh, if I'd have had any time, uh, I mean, I mean, I, I'd run over them and I'd play those numbers. I still have them in mind and when they're in your mind, you can, it don't take no more than a short time to come in. But those kind of numbers, the piano has to be in fair shape. Now, uh, uh, this, this piano, as I said before, it's all damp. It's in, it's pretty good piano. Uh, it has to be for the stoutness water. It's been underwater, halfway underwater, you know, uh, for at least, uh, two weeks. You see, it had to be. It's a Kimball. And, uh, now if I had some care, if I had got the kerosene, I'd have painted with oil and that kind of stuff. Then it would have had, action would have been there and I could have played some of those good numbers. I could have played like the Messwright Ramble and the Tiger Rag and, and, uh, some of the numbers that I was really, the diplomat blues, see, and them kind of numbers. Uh, they, they were good numbers and you could really get away with them. That's what really showed your skill in the piano. But, uh, I can't get away, get away with it, you know. No, no, no, no, no. I can't get away with it.
I'm surprised you do so wonderful things you do on that piano.

Yeah, and those beats, there was such wonderful beats. Like, see them, the diplomat blues when they come in? Mm-hm. You can't get away with it. It makes you stumble over the notes. But I'll tell you, as soon as I'm able to get this thing in shape, which it don't take too much to put it back in shape, just a little kerosene and be on it for a few hours and a couple of good dry days. And then I'm going to have the, if y'all get a chance to come back again. And then I could really play some of those numbers as they supposedly, because I got a different style. See, I didn't play all the styles that I played. I played about seven or eight different styles of piano. See, I had to do that when it'd make it warm for me. I'd get out one note and get another, see, because I'd maybe be playing in one note and those guys been out there listening. See, and they'd come on in and they'd pick
up on that. Excuse me. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And it almost swept the neighborhood away. Yeah. Sure.
If there's anything you want to do, we can stop at any time if you're busy or time for dinner.

No, no, I'm not, I'm not, I'm just going to find a tube for my. Yeah, go ahead, go ahead and look it up. Go ahead and look it up. Go ahead and look it up. Well, now let's see where you might find one. Make a little band. It is, it is, piling up some music, but then mostly, my other boys, he's mostly vocalist. He sings. Oh, yeah. Uh-huh. Yeah, he sings. And if you know his voice is, is almost like mine's. It's only, it's just a little like. Yeah. We got almost the same voice. Strange, huh? Yeah, strange. I've noticed there are sometimes too in families that runs it. Well, he, that's it. And his voice is so close to mine that I was surprised to realize, you know, one day they had a recorder here. They came out and they were singing a couple of numbers. They played this, what you call that? Rock and roll. That rock and roll music, so he was playing some of that. And he was singing a number there. And when he spoke, and I answered him on there, but when you come to find out the voice, it was so close you couldn't hardly tell, you know, who was who. And I'll tell you about this music here. If I had a chance to get out there and play me a few jobs, I would. I'd get out there and play me a few jobs because I like, you know, just to get myself back into it, see? Yeah, it would be nice if you could. And because, I mean, every now and then when I'm feeling real good, I get loose on that piano and I can feel that my fingers is just as fast as they ever was. But I still need a little practice, you know, because I might come from underneath the automobile, unscrewing some nuts and bolts, and sit out on the piano, you know, the biggest dollar type. And if I don't make those notes exactly as I want, then I'll give them a slap and walk off. Come back later on. And I'll go ahead and put some hot water and limber them up there until they get stiff. Now I go to limber them up there and I'll knock off what time I come back there and really read some sense. Really read some sense.
Hot water and limbers up your fingers?
Mm-hmm. Yeah, I'll use some really hot water, see? And then just put just a little oil on them, you know, that limbers them up. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Real nice.
Yeah, so it's wonderful how it's stayed with you, as little as you do.

That's right. And, you know, sometimes I don't touch this piano for maybe two weeks, maybe a month. Now, the way that I was playing this piano right now, I hadn't touched it in about, well, at least two weeks or something. I hadn't touched it. Because I couldn't get it. The water was too hard to get there. You see, I got this big piece of, what's that, piece of four by six there, see? Four by six, yeah. Yeah, four by six. Well, I put that there after a time and it just cleared the water so I sat on the box and went on and played that. But it was holding up pretty good until about two days ago or three days. I passed by it and I made it do that just to see if it'd stick, you know? I'd do it like that. But then hold it down. When I first got it, it had been in the rain for about a month. And all the notes was stuck. Outdoors. Outdoors. Yeah, it was outdoors, you see? They'd give it to a fella and it was outdoors. And I just took it all loose and fixed it up, see? I took it all loose. All right, son. Not too bad a tune really, considering all that. No. I wonder it's in tune at all. Let's see if I can't find one of the numbers that I used. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. That number, that's I always dream of you. That's...

Thank you. Thank you. if you ever had to practice very much? If you could get to a piano often enough to practice, or did it take much practice?

Well, I'll tell you how that was. My godmother had a piano, see? And I could only get to play it whenever, you know, her husband wasn't sleeping, or if she was in a good mood, well, then I'd get a chance to play. But other than that, I couldn't get to the piano.
I'd like to ask you one question about, about dancing. I assume most of these places where you play, there'd be people dancing.
Oh, yeah.
Did they, what kind of dances did they like to dance most? Was it slow?

It was a two-step. They usually dance on Panama. Most of the dances that they danced, that was standard. A two-step and a slow drag, and a one-step. Now, the one-step, that was a tempo played about like when I played this number. Let's see what was that number I played.
I mean, it's like a slow number?

It's a slow number. It's slower than the blues. You see, the slow drag, that was like, CC rider. CC rider. They mostly danced. That was a blues. See, that was called a slow drag. Then the tempo, just a little bit faster, was called a one-step. You danced on the one-step on that. And then behind the one-step, you had the two-step, which was, or most of the time, danced by Panama, High Society, 12th Street Rags, and numbers like that. That was fast numbers, see? That was a two-step number. That's where they'd find out if you was a good fast dancer. And then you had the waltz. That was the standard numbers. The standard numbers. Oh, yeah.
You used to play waltzes, too?
Oh, yes. Yes, indeed. I used to play all those numbers. I used to always feature this number, Peggy O'Neill. I liked it. Oh, yeah. Peggy O'Neill.
The shardest, he played, tell you how he played waltzes.

And that's what I was fixing to say. The waltz and the shardest, that was a popular dance. They contest you on the shardest. Oh, yeah? Yeah. You dance around right and left. You never stop turning. You go all the way to the other hall, and you keep turning. You never give up action. And the same way with the piano. The guy played the piano. He never let up on the beat of the number. The shardest was a hard number all the way for dancing and playing. Very few piano players played the shardest. There was only about six piano players around, I mean, of the time, that played the shardest. And that was fellas like Newman, Udell, Big Bill Thompson, myself.
Udell, what was his last name?
I don't know. What was his name?
I've heard of Udell.
Yeah, he, he.
That's Udell from St. Louis. He's talking about that.

Or Kansas City. Yeah. Kansas City. Yeah. I meant to say Kansas City. Is that the fella? Yeah. He used to be in New Orleans pretty much, see? Yeah. He was in the same. That's the same fella. That's the same fella, yeah. That's the same one he's talking about. Yeah, he used to be in New Orleans pretty much. Well, that was most of the guys that played the shards. Yeah, I guess that's the end of the story. Thank you.
